challenges.name: is-it-really-faster
challenges.title: Is it really faster? Read the runs
challenges.description: The perf bot said PR #1042 made GET /api/leaderboard 11% faster, from one run of each build. Two statements on that comment and on an A/A check of the unchanged code: what one run per side can and cannot tell you.

questions.question:
PR #1042 "leaderboard: cache rank lookups" - comment from the perf bot
(k6, GET /api/leaderboard on staging, 150 req/s for 60 s, one run per build):
  main     http_req_duration p(95)=212ms
  branch   http_req_duration p(95)=188ms   -11.3%  FASTER

A/A check the next morning: the same commit of main (8c41d2e), five runs back to back,
same k6 script, same staging host, nothing changed between runs:
  run 1  p(95)=196ms
  run 2  p(95)=231ms
  run 3  p(95)=188ms
  run 4  p(95)=214ms
  run 5  p(95)=205ms

Statement: "The 24 ms gap reported on PR #1042 is smaller than the spread between runs of unchanged code, so these two runs alone cannot tell whether the change made the endpoint faster."
questions.explanation: True. With no code change at all, the p95 of main moved between 188 and 231 ms, a 43 ms spread; run 3 of main even matched the branch's 188 ms exactly. A 24 ms gap between one run of each build fits inside that noise, so it could come from the run, not from the change. This does not prove the cache is useless: it means one run per side cannot separate the change from the noise. You need several runs per build, interleaved, and an interval for the difference. The misconception is to read a percentage with a FASTER label as a measured effect.

questions.question:
k6 end-of-test summaries of the two runs behind PR #1042 (trimmed):
  main    http_reqs: 9000   http_req_duration: avg=97.4ms med=81ms p(95)=212ms
  branch  http_reqs: 9000   http_req_duration: avg=94.1ms med=80ms p(95)=188ms

Five A/A runs of main on the same host, 9,000 requests each, gave p(95) values from 188 ms to 231 ms.

Statement: "Each p95 is computed from 9,000 requests, so it is precise to a few milliseconds; with that many samples per run, the 24 ms gap between the two runs is a real improvement."
questions.explanation: False. 9,000 samples describe that one run precisely, but every request in a run shares the run's conditions: what else ran on the staging host, the cache and buffer state, a vacuum or garbage collection that happened to start, the hardware the VM landed on. Those conditions change from run to run, and the A/A check measures their effect directly: a 43 ms spread with 9,000 requests in every run. More requests per run do not shrink run-to-run variation; more runs do. Treat the run as the unit of comparison. The misconception is that a large sample count inside one run gives confidence about the difference between builds.

challenges.name: decide-if-b-is-faster
challenges.title: Decide whether build B is really faster
challenges.description:
After PR #1042 was merged on the strength of one run per build, the CodeDev team changed the perf bot: every pull request now gets at least 3 interleaved runs of main (A) and of the branch (B) against GET /api/leaderboard, and the bot posts a verdict only when the difference between the builds is larger than the run-to-run noise. Write compare_runs(case) for the bot. The runner has no load generator: the input is the recorded latencies of each run.

Input (stdin, one test case): {"a": [[latency_ms, ...], ...], "b": [[latency_ms, ...], ...], "resamples": R, "seed": S}. a and b hold one list of samples (ms) per run. R >= 1, 0 <= S < 2**31.

1. p95 of each run, nearest rank (the definition used in the whole course): sort the run's samples, rank = ceil(95/100 x n), p95 = sorted[rank - 1]. Compute the rank with integers to stay exact: (95 * n + 99) // 100.
2. diff = mean(p95s of A) - mean(p95s of B). Positive means B is faster.
3. Bootstrap over runs: the run is the unit, never a single sample. PRNG: state starts at S; next() sets state = (1103515245 * state + 12345) % 2**31 and returns the new state; drawing from a list of k values picks the value at index next() % k. For each of the R resamples, in this order: draw len(a) values from A's p95 list (with replacement), then len(b) values from B's p95 list; the resample's difference is mean(drawn A) - mean(drawn B). The state carries over from one resample to the next.
4. Sort the R differences. The 95% interval is [low, high] = their nearest-rank 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles: rank = (25 * R + 999) // 1000 and (975 * R + 999) // 1000, value = sorted[rank - 1].
5. verdict: "B is faster" if low > 0, "B is slower" if high < 0, otherwise "no clear difference".

Output: {"p95_a": [per run, in input order], "p95_b": [...], "diff_ms": diff, "ci_ms": [low, high], "verdict": ...}. Round diff_ms, low and high to 1 decimal with round(); decide the verdict on the unrounded values.
Errors, checked in this order: {"error": "need at least 3 runs per side"} when a or b has fewer than 3 runs; {"error": "empty run"} when any run has no samples.

Example: A's runs have p95s 210, 215 and 205 ms and B's 150, 160 and 155 ms: diff_ms is 55.0, every resample difference is positive, and the verdict is "B is faster".
hints: The A/A check gave five p95s of unchanged code between 188 and 231 ms. If you poured the samples of those five runs into one big list, where would that 43 ms spread go - and what would that do to the width of your interval?

Three places decide most of the output: the rank in p95 (an integer ceiling, 1-based), the order of the PRNG draws (all of A's draws of a resample come before B's, and the state is never reset between resamples), and the verdict, which looks only at the two ends of the interval, never at diff_ms. Check the run count before the empty runs.

The same steps on other numbers: A's p95 list [10, 20, 30], B's [5, 15, 25], seed 1. next() gives 1103527590, 377401575 and 662824084; modulo 3 these are 0, 0 and 1, so A draws 10, 10, 20 (mean 13.33). Then 1147902781, 2035015474 and 368800899 give 1, 1, 0, so B draws 15, 15, 5 (mean 11.67): this resample's difference is 1.67. With R = 40 resamples, the interval ends are the 1st and the 39th sorted differences. And a run of 19 samples has rank ceil(18.05) = 19: its p95 is its largest sample.

tests.name: Clear win: B's p95 is lower than A's in every run
The incident: runs overlap, so a 1-run gap is no clear difference
Regression: B is slower in every run, the interval is below zero
A/A: identical runs on both sides give a zero interval
Nearest-rank p95 on runs of 1, 2, 19, 20 and 21 samples; 7 resamples
Only 2 runs of B: an error, not a verdict

expected.error: need at least 3 runs per side

tests.name: A run with no samples is an error
Large: 12 runs of 400 samples per side, 2,000 resamples
